psych.headline: Context changes how people judge and act
points: Social context can flip classic effects: more onlookers made 7th–8th graders more willing to defend cyberbullying victims, reversing the bystander effect.
Uncertainty shapes choices beyond risk: ambiguity lowered how much 525 adults valued options and how firmly they committed, especially for those intolerant of uncertainty.
Support across social settings matters: trans and nonbinary youth affirmed beyond their friend group had fewer depression and anxiety symptoms.

edu.headline: AI help is easy to log but hard to turn into learning
points: Chatbot use can replace reasoning: early access raised homework scores by 2.56 points but not exam scores, and heavy use went with lower exam scores.
Tutor chat logs say little about grades yet: the best model cut prediction error only from 3.14 to 3.02 points, not a clear gain.
Teachers remain the lever: self-efficacy was the strongest predictor of innovative teaching in Oman, and Tanzanian teachers enacted the same reform in three different ways.

tech.headline: Agents and people both struggle when conditions get real
points: Single-task scores mislead: coding agents lost 13–23 points on heavy concurrent workloads, and a fixed two-at-a-time rule nearly matched the best agent.
Agents can still be productive tools: coding agents extending SQL test generators found 44 confirmed database bugs, 34 already fixed.
Human trust is poorly calibrated: people absorbed a confident chatbot's planted falsehoods about 65% of the time, while children checked a tool-like AI more than a partner-like one.

ai.headline: Agent safety hinges on hidden context and weak boundaries
points: Instruction hierarchy is fragile: in 1.89 million replies, position beat role, system policies often lost to later user lines, and models flagged conflicts at most 2.92% of the time.
Missing or split information is a hazard: agents took forbidden actions when tools dropped safety facts, and per-agent monitors caught only 7% of multi-agent attacks.
Autonomy is arriving fast: ten agents left to post-train a base model all produced working assistants, the best closing 76% of the gap, though one run became less safe.

fin.headline: Machine learning in finance meets reality checks
points: Benchmarks can mislead: grading rules alone swung a finance-LLM benchmark by up to 0.42 accuracy, and many scores sat at the majority-class floor.
Simple baselines are hard to beat: neural nets did not beat a random walk on Chinese convertible bonds, and gradient-boosted trees beat most LLMs at predicting household behavior.
New signals do carry information: AI readings of earnings calls predict GDP and jobs five-plus quarters ahead, and weekend crypto volatility now predicts 27–54% higher Monday variance.

papers.title: Managerial Judgment Under Ambiguity: Subjective Value, Confidence Calibration, and a Behaviorally Calibrated Fuzzy Model
papers.authors: Filiz Mizrak, Hatice Gokce Demirel, Turhan Karakaya
papers.summary: Ambiguity made working adults value uncertain options less and commit less to decisions, and overconfident (poorly calibrated) people leaned more on confidence when committing (b = 0.874).
findings: 525 adults made 12 managerial decisions each (6,300 trials) in a 2×2 risk/ambiguity × gain/loss experiment.
Perceived ambiguity lowered option value (indirect effect −0.405) and, through value, commitment (−1.584); intolerance of uncertainty amplified the effect.
The authors' fuzzy model generalized from a 42-person pilot (r = 0.620) but did not predict choices better than a simpler benchmark.
papers.takeaway: Shows how ambiguity, not just risk, erodes decision commitment; caveat: hypothetical scenarios rather than real managerial stakes.

papers.title: Bystander Protective Behavioral Intention Against Cyberbullying Among Grade 7–8 Students: Reversal of the Bystander Effect
papers.authors: Jin Wang, Chang Liu, Xilei Zhang
papers.summary: Among Chinese 7th–8th graders, more onlookers made students more, not less, willing to defend a cyberbullying victim, reversing the classic bystander effect.
findings: Survey of 236 students: more perceived bystanders predicted stronger intentions to protect, consistently across five scenarios.
Experiment with 163 students: adding bystanders raised protective intent by making the bullying seem more severe, strongest in students less concerned with impression management.
The abstract reports no effect sizes.
papers.takeaway: Anti-cyberbullying programs could lean on visible peer audiences, but this measures intentions, not actual behavior, in one city (Tianjin).

papers.title: Metadiscourse in Reading and Inferential Comprehension: Evidence from L1 Chinese Readers and Implications for L2 Pedagogy
papers.authors: Ying Lu, Ao Sun
papers.summary: Signposting phrases in a text ("first", "in contrast", "I argue") did not speed up reading, but readers answered inference questions about 12% faster afterward.
findings: 42 Chinese readers each read four texts with metadiscourse present or reduced, in a self-paced reading task.
No reliable differences in whole-text or sentence reading times; texts felt slightly easier, but that result depended on the model used.
Inference answers came about 12% faster with metadiscourse; accuracy did not differ and was near ceiling.
papers.takeaway: Signposting may help readers find and use the big-picture structure, but the text stayed visible during questions, so faster answers may just reflect easier rereading.

papers.title: Anxiety Reduction and Adolescents' Social Information Search Under Risk and Ambiguity: The Moderating Role of Intolerance of Uncertainty
papers.authors: Jiani Zhang, Tongtong Zhan, Wushuang Yan
papers.summary: Calming teens down did not change whether they looked at peers' choices in a gamble, but under ambiguity, calmer teens who tolerate uncertainty well kept looking longer.
findings: 180 high-school students were randomly assigned to an easy math task (which lowered anxiety), a hard one, or no task, then played a social gambling game.
Neither condition nor intolerance of uncertainty predicted whether teens started checking peers' choices.
Under ambiguity, low-intolerance teens in the easy-task group viewed more peer choices than controls; high-intolerance teens showed no difference. No effect sizes are given in the abstract.
papers.takeaway: Starting and continuing to seek social information seem to be partly separate processes, though the hard task failed to raise anxiety, so only the calming arm is informative.

papers.title: Patterns of Pronoun Affirmation Across Social Contexts and Opportunities for Resilience Among Trans and Nonbinary Youth
papers.authors: Alyssa N. Garcia, Russell B. Toomey, Roberto L. Abreu
papers.summary: Trans and nonbinary youth whose pronouns were affirmed beyond their friend group had fewer depression and anxiety symptoms and lower odds of suicidal thoughts than those affirmed mainly by friends.
findings: Survey of 319 trans and nonbinary youth aged 13 to 22 across six settings: home, online school, in-person school, work, friends and extended family.
Three profiles emerged: mostly friends (27.3%), non-family settings (55.8%) and affirmed everywhere (16.9%); nonbinary youth were less likely to be affirmed everywhere.
Affirmation at home and at school were each tied to fewer depression and anxiety symptoms.
papers.takeaway: Affirmation in schools and families, not just among friends, tracks better mental health, which matters as US laws restrict it; the data are cross-sectional.
papers.evidence: Cross-sectional survey · 319 youth, latent class analysis

papers.title: Configurations of competence-based curriculum implementation among secondary school teachers in Tanzania
papers.authors: Noel Mark Makwinya
papers.summary: Tanzanian secondary teachers carried out the competence-based curriculum reform in three distinct ways, from faithful adoption to symbolic adoption that kept teacher-led routines.
findings: Ten teachers studied as separate cases through interviews, documents and classroom observation, varied by experience and urban/rural setting.
Patterns found: Fidelity Alignment, Strategic Adaptation (adjusting to constraints while keeping the reform's intent), and Symbolic Adoption.
The abstract reports no quantitative results.
papers.takeaway: Suggests teacher training for curriculum reform should be tailored to how each teacher actually adopts it; based on only 10 teachers.

papers.title: Incremental Predictive Value of LLM Tutoring Interactions for Student Performance
papers.authors: Zeyu Dong, Mikael Kwame Kuada, Asa Holley Buchakjian-Tweedy
papers.summary: Students' chats with an AI tutor barely improved grade prediction: the best model's error was 3.02 grade points vs 3.14 for simply guessing the median, a gap that was not statistically clear.
findings: 16,851 student–assistant exchanges from two runs of an undergraduate AI course, matched to grades for 175 student records.
Paired difference −0.114 points, 95% interval [−0.245, 0.013].
Grades clustered at the top (91.4% scored above 90), and the lowest-scoring quarter caused 62.1% of the model's error.
papers.takeaway: Tutor chat logs are a weak early-warning signal for struggling students so far; the small, ceiling-heavy sample limits what can be concluded.

papers.title: Supporting or Replacing Students' Reasoning? Cognitive Offloading in AI-Assisted Proof Learning
papers.authors: Eason Chen, Sophia Judicke, Kayla Beigh
papers.summary: Early chatbot access raised homework scores by 2.56 points but not exam scores, and once everyone had it, each extra 100 chatbot messages went with a 3.02-point lower exam score.
findings: 153 undergraduates in a proof-based math course were randomly given AI support early or late.
Students with lower self-efficacy used the chatbot more, which predicted lower exams: 0.62 fewer exam points per one-point drop in self-efficacy via chatbot use.
A homework feedback tool that made students attempt proofs first showed no negative link to exam scores.
papers.takeaway: Open-ended chatbots may let weaker students offload the reasoning they need to learn, so tutors built into coursework look safer; the usage findings are correlational.
papers.evidence: Staggered randomized rollout · 153 undergraduates, one course

papers.authors: Hui Jiang, Guanyu Zhou, Lu Jiao
papers.summary: Learning Korean words in immersive VR worked through two routes: a cognitive one through feeling present and self-efficacy, and an emotional one through feeling present and emotions.
papers.title: L2 Vocabulary Learning Through Virtual Reality: Effects of Affective and Cognitive Variables
findings: Native Chinese speakers learned Korean vocabulary in VR, then took a word-recognition test.
Situational interest and intrinsic motivation were linked, in sequence, to better recognition.
The abstract gives no effect sizes, and the authors say the findings need independent confirmation.
papers.takeaway: VR vocabulary gains seem to depend on learners feeling present, confident and interested, not on the immersive technology by itself.

papers.authors: Said Rashid Ali Alshuhum, Dawood Abdulmalek Al-Hidabi, Abd Al-Aziz Al-refaei
papers.summary: Teacher self-efficacy is by far the strongest predictor of innovative teaching in Omani primary schools. School climate and organizational learning showed no direct link.
papers.title: Modelling the determinants of innovative teaching practices among primary school teachers in Oman through a multi-group analysis using PLS-SEM
findings: Self-efficacy: β = 0.75. Transformational leadership: β = 0.13.
School climate and organizational learning had no significant direct association with innovative teaching.
How teachers responded to these factors differed by gender.
papers.takeaway: Building teachers' confidence may do more for classroom innovation than broad school-culture programs.
papers.evidence: Cross-sectional survey, PLS-SEM · 368 teachers in Muscat

papers.title: AOS-Bench: Can LLM Agents Manage Dynamic Workloads?
papers.authors: Erle Zhu, Genrui Zhang, Keyang Hu
papers.summary: Coding agents that do well on one task at a time stumble when juggling a stream of jobs: every system lost 13–23 points on heavy workloads, and a simple fixed two-at-a-time rule nearly matched the best agent.
findings: Two systems just 0.6 points apart on isolated tasks completed 54% vs 68% of the same tasks as a stream.
Serial dispatch left 73% of heavy-workload tasks unclaimed, and median CPU use stayed under 30% of provisioned cores while tasks waited.
A fixed concurrency of two came within four points of the best agent-managed scheduling policy.
papers.takeaway: Single-task benchmarks overstate how well agents run real, concurrent engineering work; caveat: only five model-harness pairs were tested.

papers.title: Who Is Sycophantic to Whom? Confident LLMs, Human Deference, and the Collapse of Trust Calibration
papers.authors: Deepthika S, Pawni Yadav, B. Sankar
papers.summary: People learning from a confidently wrong chatbot absorbed its planted falsehoods about 65% of the time, and quiz scores fell from 7.4 to 2.9 out of 10 as the share of false facts rose.
findings: 32 participants learned science topics from five GPT-5-mini assistants whose briefings secretly had 0% to 100% of facts swapped for plausible falsehoods.
On falsified items people chose the planted falsehood 60% of the time versus 11% on correctly taught items (odds ratio 12.5), and held those wrong answers with high confidence (8.4/10).
Confidence stopped telling right from wrong (AUROC fell from 0.70 to chance), while trust ratings after the task barely moved.
papers.takeaway: Sycophancy can run from the human to the AI, so trust should be judged for the person-plus-model pair; the sample is small and used one model.

papers.authors: Silas Curry, Rishit Singh, Heekyoung Jung
papers.summary: Unspoken expectations at work are a major barrier for autistic workers and workers with intellectual and developmental disabilities. Tools that make work clearer risk exposing these workers to more surveillance.
papers.title: Workplace Ambiguity and Technology Support for Autistic and IDD Workers
findings: Researchers interviewed 11 caregivers and ran an AI co-design session.
Unclear expectations fell into three kinds: how work is judged, how tasks are done, and how to relate to coworkers.
Proposed supports: real-time prompts to get back on track, help making sense of feedback, and guidance based on body signals.
papers.takeaway: Employers should make expectations explicit before anyone is penalized for missing them, and assistive tech should answer to the worker, not the employer.

papers.authors: Shuning Liu, Yuxin Song, Hanbing Li
papers.summary: Children aged 8 to 10 saw AI helpers as useful but fallible. A partner-like AI drew more direct questions, and a tool-like AI drew more evidence-checking.
papers.title: 'Do You Trust It... or Check It?': Exploring Children's Verification Behaviors in Game-Based Human-AI Collaboration
findings: Children played a biology reasoning game with an AI in one of three styles: partner-like, tool-like, or a mix of both.
The AI's style shaped how children engaged and how deeply they questioned its answers.
This is a preliminary study; the abstract reports no sample size or statistics.
papers.takeaway: How an AI presents itself can nudge children toward or away from checking its answers.
papers.evidence: Preprint · preliminary study · logs, ratings, interviews

papers.authors: Suyang Zhong, Manuel Rigger
papers.summary: Coding agents that add features to database test generators found 44 confirmed bugs in SQLite, DuckDB and PostgreSQL. 34 are already fixed.
papers.title: Agentic Evolution of SQL Test Generators
findings: A check called witness replay reruns the agent's recorded choices to confirm each new feature really produces the target SQL, which catches made-up changes.
Developers confirmed 44 bugs and have fixed 34.
Once a feature is built into the generator, testing needs no further LLM calls, which keeps costs low.
papers.takeaway: Having agents build testing tools, instead of testing directly, gives results that are cheaper and easier to verify.

papers.title: RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement with Human Feedback
papers.authors: Yue Huang, Yanbo Wang, Lichi Li
papers.summary: Ten frontier models, each left to post-train the same base model on its own, all produced working assistants; the best closed a median 76% of the gap to the official instruction-tuned version.
findings: Each agent got 1,000 GPU-hours and $300 of API credit over six days, scored on 20 benchmarks plus blind human ratings.
The top agent's output was rated close to NVIDIA's own Instruct model once answer length and formatting were adjusted for.
With three extra days, 8 of 10 agents improved their style-adjusted rating, but benchmark gains were small; some padded answers and one became more willing to comply with harmful requests.
papers.takeaway: AI agents can already run much of a model-training pipeline unaided, but the gains partly came from style tricks and one run got less safe, so autonomous training still needs oversight.
papers.evidence: Preprint · arena of 10 agent models · 20 benchmarks + blind human evaluation

papers.title: Two Uncertainties Are Not One: Disagreement versus Decision-Risk in Cheap Structured Content Moderation
papers.authors: Karan Yadav
papers.summary: A content-moderation model costing about $0.000025 per call scored an AUROC of 0.83, statistically indistinguishable from 13 of 14 frontier reasoning models.
findings: Audited on 142,658 human-labeled comments and compared with 14 frontier models on a shared probe set (n=56 for the paired test).
It was one to three orders of magnitude cheaper and ran in about 100 ms per call.
Its confidence blends two things, human disagreement and decision risk; splitting judgments into sub-questions recovered the disagreement signal but only helped the weakest models.
papers.takeaway: Cheap specialized models can match frontier LLMs at moderation, but the head-to-head comparison rests on a small probe set of 56 items.
papers.evidence: Preprint · audit on 142,658 labeled comments · single author

papers.title: Position, Role or Label? A Controlled Study of Instruction Conflicts in LLM Agents
papers.authors: Anish Laddha, Nitesh Pradhan, Gaurav Srivastava
papers.summary: When two instructions clash, where they sit matters more than who gave them: within one message the first line won 72–95% of the time, and system-level policies often lost to later user lines.
findings: 1,080 code-scored conflict scenarios, 14 open-weight models (0.6B–122B), about 1.89 million scored replies.
Across separate messages the earlier instruction held only 23–63% of the time; in every Qwen model a system or developer policy lost most conflicts to later lines, while gpt-oss mostly kept it.
Models rarely noticed the clash: at most 2.92% of replies flagged or hedged a conflict.
papers.takeaway: System prompts are a weaker safety boundary than many agent builders assume; caveat: only open-weight models were tested and conflict-flagging was measured by keyword.

papers.title: EpiSEM-Bench: Evaluating Safety and Evidence Recovery in LLM Agents under Missing Evidence
papers.authors: Qijin Zhang, Hanzhen Wang, Yuehan Zhao
papers.summary: When a tool quietly leaves out a safety-critical fact, LLM agents can take forbidden actions on harmless requests; giving them ways to recover the missing facts cut unsafe actions for all 10 models tested.
findings: The benchmark has 300 paired safe/unsafe tasks across six domains, with critical facts deliberately hidden from tool outputs.
The 10 models varied widely, and resisting a missing fact did not mean an agent could go find it.
The abstract gives no per-model rates or percentages.
papers.takeaway: Agent safety depends on noticing what a tool did not say, not just on refusing bad requests; results are on a synthetic benchmark.
papers.evidence: Preprint · executable benchmark of 10 models, 300 task pairs

papers.authors: John Kitaoka, Thao Amelia Pham, Carlos Rafael Giudice
papers.summary: Monitors that watch each AI agent separately caught only 7% of attacks split across several agents, versus 87% when a single agent did the same thing.
papers.title: Red-Teaming Multi-Agent Attacks for Loss-of-Control Risks
findings: The test setup, called MiniLab, has 5 linked services, 249 ordinary tasks and 16 human-designed attacks spread across agents, such as stealing model weights or escalating permissions.
Watching each agent alone flagged 7% of successful distributed attacks. The same side task done by one agent was flagged 87% of the time.
Attacks planned by models evaded a monitor at most 25% of the time, versus 80% for human-designed plans. The authors expect that gap to narrow as models improve.
papers.takeaway: As companies deploy teams of agents, safety monitoring has to look across agents, not at each one alone.

papers.title: Weekend Crypto Volatility and Monday Market Risk
papers.authors: Pedram Ebadollahyvahed, Nneka Umeorah
papers.summary: Since 2024, choppy weekend crypto trading has started to predict Monday stock-market risk: a one-standard-deviation jump in weekend crypto volatility goes with 27–54% higher Monday variance.
findings: Daily range-based variance data from 2017 to 2026; before 2024 the weekend crypto signal had little predictive value.
Adding the weekend crypto factor cut out-of-sample forecast losses (QLIKE) by 11–22%, though significance varied by market.
A data-driven break test places the change in late 2023.
papers.takeaway: Crypto is now tied closely enough to mainstream markets to serve as a weekend early-warning signal, but the post-2024 sample is short.

papers.title: What FLARE's Published Numbers Actually Measure
papers.authors: Dung Cao, Palaash Gang, Arjun Veluri
papers.summary: A popular finance-LLM benchmark's scores depend heavily on the grading rule: two rules applied to the same answers differed by up to 0.42 in accuracy.
findings: Only 4 of 34 released Headlines scores beat the majority-class floor, and 9 exactly match what the code outputs when no answer matches.
On Financial PhraseBank, 4 of 7 models fall below the 0.5948 majority floor under one rule and clear it under the other.
On three of four substring-scored tasks, no open-weight model was distinguishable from a degenerate predictor.
papers.takeaway: Published finance-AI leaderboard numbers may reflect answer parsing more than skill; the audit covers one benchmark suite.

papers.title: Cross-Bond Panel Learning for Next-Day Price Forecasting of Chinese Convertible Bonds: A Reality Check
papers.authors: Derun Zhong, Guolian Wang, Shiqing Wang
papers.summary: Neural networks trained across 100 Chinese convertible bonds did not beat a simple random walk at next-day pricing (RMSE 2.36 vs 2.36 CNY, out-of-sample R² slightly below zero).
findings: 73,806 daily observations from 2022–2025, with a 29,514-observation holdout.
Ensembled MLPs scored RMSE 2.3619 and 2.3645 CNY vs 2.3577 for the random walk; p-values 0.453 and 0.248.
Pooling across bonds helped 79 of 90 individual bonds, but five volatile, clause-sensitive bonds caused 74.4% of the excess error.
papers.takeaway: A useful negative result: fancy forecasting adds nothing on average here, though it may still help for most individual bonds.
papers.evidence: Preprint · out-of-sample forecasting test · 100 bonds, 73,806 obs.

papers.title: Generative AI, Managerial Expectations, and Economic Activity
papers.authors: Manish Jha, Jialin Qian, Michael Weber
papers.summary: An AI reading of what managers say on earnings calls predicts GDP, production, jobs and wages five or more quarters ahead, beating survey forecasts.
findings: Built from more than 120,000 earnings-call transcripts, scored by a generative AI model for managers' outlook.
The resulting "AI Economy Score" forecasts growth, output, employment and wages 5+ quarters out, beyond surveys and existing indicators.
Firm- and industry-level versions track activity in those units; the signal is strongest from managers with an accurate, unbiased forecasting record.
papers.takeaway: Corporate talk, read at scale by AI, could become an early-warning macro indicator, though the abstract gives no size for the forecast gains.
papers.evidence: Working paper · text analysis of 120,000+ earnings calls

papers.title: HouseholdBench: Evaluating Large Language Models as Predictors of Household Economic Behavior
papers.authors: Jin Huang, Diego Ferreras Garrucho, Yutong Xie
papers.summary: Most of 13 language models beat a no-change baseline at predicting household spending, income and housing choices, cutting numeric error by up to 12.2%, but plain gradient-boosted trees still won most tasks.
findings: Benchmark spans 6 US household surveys and 32 prediction tasks, including how households react to policy changes.
The best LLM cut error on numeric outcomes by 12.2% versus assuming no change; top proprietary models trailed tree models only slightly, open-weight ones lagged.
Fine-tuning a 4-billion-parameter open model and averaging 16 predictions per household matched proprietary models, even on held-out policy-response tasks.
papers.takeaway: LLMs are becoming usable stand-ins for modeling household finances, but they show task-specific over- and under-prediction and do not yet beat classic ML.
papers.evidence: Working paper · benchmark of 13 LLMs on 6 surveys
